summary:
Each pixel becomes the rounded-down average of the in-bounds pixels of its 3 × 3 block, all computed from
the **original** photo. Reading from a copy is simplest; to avoid the copy, store each new value in the
unused high bits of its cell and shift them down at the end.

question.md:
Replace every pixel by the average (rounded down) of the pixels in the 3 × 3 block centred on it,
counting only pixels inside the photo.

- **Different pixels average different counts:** a corner averages 4 pixels, an edge pixel 6, an inner
  pixel 9. A 1 × 1 photo averages just itself.
- **All averages use the original values**, never already-softened neighbours.
- **Rounded down:** integer division.
- **Values 0 … 255** fit in 8 bits, leaving plenty of spare bits in an `int`.

think.md:
Take a 3 × 3 photo with a bright centre (250). The centre averages all 9 pixels: 650 / 9 → 72. The corner
(0, 0) averages only its 4-pixel block: 10 + 20 + 40 + 250 = 320, 320 / 4 = 80.

think.caption: The corner's block has 4 pixels; the centre's has 9.

think.md:
If you overwrote pixels as you go, the next pixel's block would include a softened value, which is
wrong. So, as with any "simultaneous" grid update, either read from a copy, or keep the original value
recoverable inside the cell (`value & 255`) while the new one sits in higher bits (`value >> 8`).

approaches.title: Average from a copy

idea.md: Keep the original photo untouched and write each average into a new grid. For every pixel, add up the in-bounds block and divide by how many pixels it had.

build: For each pixel, sum the original values in rows r−1 … r+1 and columns c−1 … c+1 that are inside the photo, counting them.

lines.text: A fresh grid for the results, so the original stays readable.
Add up the 3 × 3 block clipped to the photo, and count how many pixels it really has (4, 6 or 9; fewer for very thin photos).
Integer division rounds down, as required.

notes.c: Report the row count and each row's length.

complexity.md: **Time O(m · n):** at most 9 reads per pixel. **Space O(m · n)** for the output grid.

steps.text: Pixel (0, 0): 4 pixels in its block sum to 320; 320 // 4 = 80.
Pixel (0, 1): 6 pixels in its block sum to 410; 410 // 6 = 68.
Pixel (1, 1): 9 pixels in its block sum to 650; 650 // 9 = 72.
Pixel (2, 2): 4 pixels in its block sum to 480; 480 // 4 = 120.
Every pixel computed from the original values.

walk.title: Average each pixel's 3 × 3 block in the original photo, clipped at the edges.

limits.md: A whole second grid, while each pixel uses only 8 of its cell's 32 bits. The new value fits in the spare bits.

approaches.title: Pack the new value into the high bits

idea.md:
A pixel value fits in bits 0 … 7. During one pass, read neighbours as `value & 255` (only the
original bits) and store each average in bits 8 … 15 with `value |= avg << 8`. Reads never see
the stored averages. A second pass `value >>= 8` keeps only the new values.

build: For each pixel, sum `image[rr][cc] & 255` over its clipped block, and count the pixels.
Afterwards shift every cell right by 8.

lines.text: `& 255` keeps only the low 8 bits: the **original** pixel, even for neighbours that already carry their new value above.
Store the average (also 0 … 255) in bits 8 … 15. The low 8 bits are left alone for pixels still to come.
Drop the old 8 bits; the new value moves down into place.

notes.c: Only the column-size array is new memory.

steps.text: Pass 1: every average is computed from `value & 255` (the original 8 bits) and stored as `avg << 8`, i.e. avg × 256 added on top.
Pass 2: shift every cell right by 8 bits, leaving only the new value.

walk.title: Pixels use 8 bits (0 … 255). Store each new value in bits 8 … 15 of the same cell; shift down at the end.

takeaways.md:
- Simultaneous grid updates: read old, write new. A copy is easiest; packing old and new into one cell
  saves the memory.
- `& mask` reads the old bits, `<< k` stores the new value above them, `>> k` finishes the job.
- At borders, count how many cells you actually averaged; don't divide by 9 blindly.
